title: Oprah Winfrey sparks fresh backlash after she revisits Prince Harry and Meghan Markle bombshell interview
summary: Oprah Winfrey explains her unscripted "silent or silenced" question to Meghan Markle as critics accuse her of rewriting history years later.
story: Hugo Vickers, author of "Queen Elizabeth II: A Personal History," details how the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's exit and Oprah interview added strain during the late monarch's final years.
Oprah Winfrey is facing a new wave of backlash over an old royal bombshell.
After revisiting her 2021 interview with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, Winfrey's explanation of her "silent or silenced" question has sparked renewed debate online.

The media mogul's reflection on one of the most talked-about moments from the explosive sit-down has reignited debate over the interview that shook the monarchy, divided viewers and put Harry and Meghan's claims about royal life under a global microscope.
MEGHAN MARKLE, PRINCE HARRY'S INTERVIEW WITH OPRAH WINFREY: 6 BIGGEST BOMBSHELLS
Oprah Winfrey interviewed Prince Harry and Meghan Markle for a special in 2021 where they revealed their struggles with royal life. (Harpo Productions/Joe Pugliese via Getty Images)

During a recent Vanity Fair interview, Winfrey looked back on the viral exchange with Meghan, explaining why she challenged the Duchess of Sussex after she said she had been "silent" during her time as a working royal.

"I wanted to be clear because was she silenced? Were people telling her not to talk?... I said it for clarification because I didn't want later to hear, 'Well, no, it wasn't that. It really was that I was silenced. They wouldn't let me talk.' So it was all for clarification."
Meghan told Winfrey at the time, "I've always valued independence" and "I've always been outspoken, especially about women's rights."
"I mean, that's the sad irony of the last four years is I've advocated for so long for women to use their voice. And then, I was silent."
Winfrey responded with the question that instantly went viral.
"Were you silent or were you silenced?"
"The latter," Meghan replied.
Winfrey also revealed that Harry and Meghan did not know what questions she planned to ask before the interview.
"They didn't know obviously anything that I was going to ask them, but I had said to them ahead of time, 'I'm going to try to cover everything.'"
"This interview took three and a half hours... I was just trying to carefully go through everything that had come up in the past."
Oprah Winfrey sparks royal backlash after revisiting her viral 'silenced' question to Meghan Markle. (Chris Jackson - Pool/Getty Images)

The 2021 CBS special became one of the biggest celebrity interviews of the decade after Harry and Meghan opened up about their decision to step away from royal duties, allegations of a lack of support from the royal family, Meghan's mental health struggles, and claims about conversations surrounding their son Archie's royal status and security.
The couple's comments sparked worldwide debate, including Meghan's claim that there were "concerns and conversations" about "how dark his skin might be when he's born."
Harry also described feeling trapped within the royal institution.
"I need to do this for my family. This is not a surprise to anybody," he said.
QUEEN ELIZABETH CALLS FOR UNITY AHEAD OF MEGHAN MARKLE, PRINCE HARRY INTERVIEW IN COMMONWEALTH DAY SPEECH
"It's really sad that it's got to this point, but I've got to do something for my own mental health, for my wife's, and for Archie's as well, because I could see where this was headed."
Winfrey's latest comments quickly triggered a wave of reactions online.
"Oprah backpedaling?" one X user wrote.

Another critic commented, "Oh, Oprah… You failed to challenge obvious inconsistencies… and handed Harry and Meghan a worldwide stage to tell 'their story' without proper scrutiny or questioning. Now you want 'clarification?' That ship sailed! Spare me…"
Oprah Winfrey reignites backlash over the bombshell Prince Harry royal interview. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle sit with their son Archie during their 2019 tour in Cape Town, South Africa.  (Samir Hussein)

title: Michael J. Fox says going public with Parkinson's was 'hell' on wife Tracy Pollan
summary: Michael J. Fox reveals the toll going public with his Parkinson's diagnosis has taken on wife Tracy Pollan and why he refused to hide his condition from the world.
story: Deborah W. Brooks told Fox News Digital the foundation has ‘committed over $3 billion dollars worth of research worldwide.’
Michael J. Fox is opening up about how going public with his battle with Parkinson's has affected not only him, but his loved ones.

As part of the third annual Social Impact Summit, hosted by The Hollywood Reporter and Social Impact Fund, the 65-year-old actor went into detail about why he chose to go public with his Parkinson's diagnosis and the toll that decision had and continues to have on his family, particularly his wife, Tracy Pollan.

"It was hell on Tracy. It was really hard on her — and it still is, because it’s always changing," he told The Hollywood Reporter. "But I said to her, ‘I have to go all the way here. No half measures.’
VINCE GILL GAVE AMY GRANT A REALITY CHECK DURING RECOVERY FROM BRAIN INJURY

"I started to understand what it was like for these people who didn’t have the options or the choices I had, didn’t have the connections and the reason to be optimistic ... I needed to normalize it and just be that all the time. I said, ‘I have to not hide this. F--- vanity.’"

The actor was first diagnosed with the degenerative disease in 1991 at the age of 29, keeping his diagnosis a secret for seven years, before going public in 1998 during the third season of his hit show, "Spin City."
Fox said his decision to go public with his Parkinson's diagnosis was "hell" for his wife. (Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images for The Michael J. Fox Foundation)

After one more season on the show, Fox chose to retire from acting to devote his time to advocacy and raising money for Parkinson's disease. It was then that he founded The Michael J. Fox Foundation in 2000, which is dedicated to finding a cure.

Since its inception, the foundation has generated more than $3 billion for research, which has left Fox and Deborah W. Brooks, co-Founder and CEO of the foundation, optimistic about where the research is headed.
WATCH: Co-founder of The Michael J. Fox Foundation is proud of what they have achieved

"Well, it's been the best state for Parkinson's research ever," Brooks said. "And, in large part, so much of that progress has taken place in the course of our organization's existence. Not that we're responsible for everything, but we've scaled so significantly and have been able to activate scientists globally. And that is showing in the results and the pace of progress across our field.

"We have now committed over $3 billion worth of research worldwide, and, so, we're working with scientists everywhere, and we work with academics, biotechs and pharma. Our goal is to take aha moments and get them to the drugstore shelf.

"And, so, it's been that momentum and particularly a recent breakthrough in how we can detect Parkinson's even before symptoms are the kind of things that tell us. We are onto it, and we are not giving up."
Brooks credits Fox for his courage to live his life with Parkinson's in front of the world. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)
Brooks credits Fox for his "courage and willingness to live his Parkinson's experience in front of the world," calling it "empowering for patients who face similar experiences in reducing stigma."

She also recalled her first board meeting at the foundation, noting it was clear Fox was not one to "just to put his name on something and hope for the best," and that his goal has always been "to do everything it took and get this done and close our doors."
WATCH: Deborah W. Brooks commends Michael J. Fox for his 'courage' to live openly with Parkinson's

"His purity of motive has been core to helping us think what we're going to prioritize. It shapes our values in terms of speed. Something like trying to cure diseases, that's not a time-neutral agenda item for people who have degenerative and progressive disease. And, so, I think, you know, this notion that someone puts their voice out or lends their name, it's always been deeper than that for him.

"And I see that a lot more in philanthropy in general today, but it has been a game changer. For raising awareness, of course, but it's also been a game changer to put those values to work in our mission to cure Parkinson's disease."
Brooks has seen firsthand how Fox's decision to go public with his diagnosis has helped others, saying she gets emotional thinking about his interactions with other patients.
"It is so powerful, an experience to be seen and felt when you share the experience of Parkinson's disease," she said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Fox initially retired from acting in 1998 but has since returned and is now nominated for an Emmy. (Savion Washington/FilmMagic)

While the "Back to the Future" star initially retired from acting in 1998, he returned in his first major on-screen role in 2004 for a guest appearance in "Scrubs," later starring in "The Good Wife," "Boston Legal" and "Curb Your Enthusiasm."

"It’s really prolonged my life and made my life interesting in a way that I didn’t think it would be to this point," Fox told The Hollywood Reporter. "I’m not retired from acting, but if I didn’t act again, it would be for a very good reason. I let Parkinson’s make decisions for me."
WATCH: Deborah W. Brooks gets choked up when thinking of Michael J. Fox interacting with patients
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Most recently, Fox received an Emmy nomination for his guest role on the hit Apple TV+ show, "Shrinking," in which he played a man dealing with Parkinson's who meets Harrison Ford's character, who has also been diagnosed with the disease, in a doctor's office.

"He was happy that I was sharing my experience with him as a character and helping him do what he needed to do," Fox explained. "He was so loving. I didn’t know what to expect with Harrison because he’s famously a stoic, curmudgeonly guy, and he’s really a sweetheart. He was so affectionate to me and so welcoming to me."
Fox guest starred on "Shrinking," portraying a patient with Parkinson's who bonded with Harrison Ford's character. (Tommaso Boddi/WireImage)
Michael J. Fox and John Mayer attend the Third Annual Social Impact Summit at DGA Theatre July 22 in Los Angeles. (Monica Schipper/Getty Images)

Fox and Brooks received the Philanthropic Organization of the Year award at this year's Social Impact Summit. Other honorees included John Mayer, who received the Philanthropist of the Year Award, and Stephen Curry and Ayesha Curry, who received the Philanthropists of the Year Award.

title: Country singer Megan Moroney swears off dating after men 'ruined' her biggest moments
summary: Megan Moroney says some of her biggest career moments were ruined by the wrong guy, revealing why she's choosing life on tour with no distractions.
story: Country music star Megan Moroney told Fox News Digital she is not ‘emotionally available’ for a romantic relationship, putting all her energy into her music career.
Megan Moroney isn't looking for love.

The country music star said some of the biggest moments of her fast-rising career were derailed by the wrong man. Now, Moroney is choosing to take a break from dating, trading romance for life on tour, time with loved ones and, as she put it, "no man, a dog."
"It’s really nice that this is one of the first tours I’ve been on where I’m not dating anyone, so I literally have no distractions," she told Cosmopolitan.
MEGAN MORONEY STUNS IN ORANGE BIKINI DURING FRIEND'S BAHAMAS BACHELORETTE
"And that sounds really silly, but there have been a lot of big moments and fun times that have been ruined by a guy for me. It’s nice to just have a clear head.

"I’m learning what I like and what I don’t like and what my goals are," she added. "It’s been cool to be so disciplined with my routines, to see what I’m capable of when everything is going like it’s supposed to."
Megan Moroney said she's taking a break from dating, explaining that some of the biggest moments of her career were overshadowed by relationships. (NDZ/Star Max/GC Images)
That doesn't mean she's sworn off dating for good — just for now.
"There is something about having a crush that’s exciting, and when my tour wraps up in October, when I’m back from Europe, I’ll maybe be on the prowl again."
Moroney said "cuffing season" might be calling her name, but life is peaceful right now.

"It’s been so nice to have my friends and family out [with me] and that not be an aspect of my life that is any sort of problem for me. … Life is peaceful. I got a dog in February. That’s what I needed all along — no man, a dog."

Moroney's decision to hit pause on dating comes after years of public speculation about her love life. The "6 Months Later" singer has been connected to a handful of high-profile country music names, including Morgan Wallen and Riley Green.
The 28-year-old rising star is known for blending witty storytelling with heartbreak-heavy lyrics.
Riley Green and Megan Moroney perform together Nov. 14, 2024. (Derek White/Getty Images for Audacy)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
While fans often try to decode the real-life inspiration behind her lyrics, Moroney said she's become more comfortable embracing the curiosity.

"In ‘Who Hurt You,’ I made it so obvious who it’s about that it was, like, you could google it, and that was the point of ‘Who Hurt You.’ In the past, I got frustrated with people," Moroney told Cosmo.

"I was trying to hint at things, and then people would be like, ‘Who is it about?’ And I was like, ‘You know what? I’m just gonna lay it out there. I might as well put his first and last name in it.’ Songwriting is fun, and it’s not meant to be taken so seriously."
WATCH: COUNTRY SINGER MEGAN MORONEY SAYS CAREER PREVENTS HER FROM FINDING ‘SOMEONE THAT I WANT TO MARRY RIGHT NOW’
Still, Moroney said she's learned not to apologize for writing from raw emotion even if listeners sometimes read more into it than she intended.
Megan Moroney revealed she's not looking for love while on tour, saying having "no distractions" has helped her stay focused on her career. (Rona Liana Ahdout for Cosmopolitan)
"It’s confidence that has grown over time, but it’s not being ashamed of how you felt. If you think it’s wrong, then OK. But this is how I felt, so here’s the song about it," Moroney said.

"I always try to explain to people that I’ve written songs about these big emotions, so they can feel huge in a song. But I could have felt that way really intensely for 10 minutes and wrote a whole song about it. And, so, in your head, you’re like, ‘Oh, this must be her whole life.’
"And it’s like, ‘Well, actually, I was just heated, and I wrote the song.’ Songs can be written from a few minutes of a feeling. So, sometimes it’s not that deep. Other times, it is that deep."

Moroney doesn't plan to shy away from documenting love, heartbreak and everything in between through her music. She said the honesty that fuels her songwriting is ultimately what keeps fans coming back.

"When I get scared of putting out a song because it’s too personal, I think about how it might help somebody, because every time I’ve done it and I’ve taken the risk, people have come up to me, and they’re like, ‘This song made me dump this guy’ and ‘This song is making me never want to go back to him,'" she recalled.
"It’s just one of those things where you have to be like, ‘F--- it. What’s the worst that could happen?’"
Megan Moroney admitted she may start dating again after her tour ends this fall, but for now she's embracing single life. (Rona Liana Ahdout for Cosmopolitan)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Megan Moroney said she's learned to prioritize her goals over romance as her country music career continues to soar. (Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images)
Moroney attended the University of Georgia before moving to Nashville to pursue music full time.

Moroney's breakthrough came in 2022 with the viral hit "Tennessee Orange," a love song that became a country radio staple and launched her into the mainstream. She released her debut album, "Lucky," in 2023.
The singer-songwriter won the ACM award for new female artist of the year and the CMA award for new artist of the year.
She later released her sophomore album, "Am I Okay?," in 2024.
Her newest musical endeavor, "Cloud 9," was released in February. Her tour began in May.

title: Ed Harris' biggest ‘Dutton Ranch’ complaint sparked a major shakeup: report
summary: Ed Harris was reportedly involved in picking the new showrunner for "Dutton Ranch" season two after claiming he felt "underused and inconsequential" in season one.
story: The "Dutton Ranch" star reflects on his family’s deep ties to Montana as the Paramount+ series premieres May 15 with two episodes, followed by weekly releases.
It seems as though Ed Harris' concerns surrounding his role in "Dutton Ranch" have been met.

According to Deadline, Harris, who recently shared he didn't have the best experience filming season one of the show, was kept in the loop and was involved in picking the show's new showrunner, Benjamin Cavell, after the show's creator and former showrunner, Chad Feehan, was let go after season one.
The decision to replace Feehan was "largely related" to how Harris' character was "underutilized," Deadline claimed.
The actor recently went viral when he shared he wanted to quit the show halfway through filming the first season, because he felt "underused and inconsequential."
‘DUTTON RANCH’ STAR ED HARRIS BLASTS PRODUCERS, SAYS HE WANTED TO VOID CONTRACT: ‘GET ME THE F--- OUT'
According to sources, Harris is going to be kept in the loop on "Dutton Ranch" from now on. (Eric Charbonneau/Apple TV via Getty Images)

"Midway through this first season, I was ready to go; I said, ‘Get me the f--- out of here,’ to tell you the truth. Because I didn’t feel like I was being used," he told Variety. "I felt a little bit misled."

He continued, "Prior to signing on for it, I was talked to quite a bit about what the season was, and what my character was going to do — and that I was one of the four main characters. And that wasn't really the case."
One of the issues he mentioned was finding out a scene they filmed involving his character, veterinarian Everett McKinney, was cut from the show.

"So, there's this scene in there … I'm talking to [Beth Dutton] at the bar, and [Rip Wheeler] comes in and says, 'OK, Everett, come on, it's your turn,'" Harris said. "I walk up to the mic, and they cut it… They cut the song out. I'm going, 'F--- you, people.'"
Harris claims producers told him the musical number would have been "too 'up' for the dark ending of the episode," adding he felt that was "enough reason to say I'm voiding my contract."

Harris says he told his team to get him out of "Dutton Ranch." (Emerson Miller/Paramount+)
He added that he took his concerns to production, but didn't mention Taylor Sheridan, the creator, writer and executive producer of "Yellowstone" and its spinoffs.

"I said, 'I'm feeling underused and inconsequential,' and they kind of went, 'Oh,'" Harris said. "I'm being told my character will have a little bit more to do [in Season 2]. I was just a little frustrated, to tell you the truth."

In the end, Harris admitted his perspective on his character changed when he watched the show, saying he thought the show was "pretty good," and that his character was still "relatively important to the story," although that wasn't how it felt while filming it.

"Dutton Ranch" premiered on Paramount + in May and serves as a continuation of "Yellowstone" after that show ended in December 2024.

title: Comedian was 'broke' in $3M house after water shut off during divorce
summary: Laura Clery's memoir details allegations against ex-husband Stephen Hilton, from cheating and drug addiction to threats that led to their custody battle.
story: Dana Perino discusses the anticipated Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce wedding, offering her perspective on marriage. She stresses that happiness in a marriage is built on mutual trust rather than extravagant costs or prenups. Perino emphasizes a commitment-first approach for couples considering long-term unions.
Laura Clery is giving fans an inside look into some of her darker moments in her memoir.

In her new memoir, "What Doesn't Kill You Makes You Hotter," the 39-year-old actress and comedian opened up about her relationship with her ex-husband, Stephen Hilton, and their tumultuous separation.

The "Shanked" star described the day she found out Hilton had allegedly been cheating on her by visiting massage parlors that seemingly offered "happy endings." She explained that "it was hard not to take it personally," as they had just been intimate earlier that day, and even though it left her feeling she wasn't "enough," she writes what she "mainly felt was hurt, and empathy toward him."

"It wouldn’t be my lack that drove Stephen to a stranger," she alleged in her memoir. "It would be his. It would be the thing we’d both tried to fill with drugs and alcohol and sex—the hole in the soul that, if we weren’t careful, could take us down to the rock bottom we both knew so well. I decided that I would meet him with grace and love and empathy, because if he was spiraling, the last thing he would need is to feel alone."
Clery opened up about the dark moments in her life in her new memoir. (Andrew Morales/SHE Media/Penske Media via Getty Images)
LAUREN SILVERMAN BREAKS SILENCE ON GETTING PREGNANT WITH SIMON COWELL'S CHILD WHILE MARRIED TO SOMEONE ELSE

After Hilton returned home, Clery allegedly confronted him, noting she was initially met with apologies and promises to call his sponsor, which left her feeling as if "Stephen and I could manage this challenge together" and eventually "move forward."

Later that night, however, she claims her ex-husband called her and allegedly began hurling insults at her, telling her, "I don’t have a problem. This is your fault! You’re just so f---ing controlling!" Following the phone call, she checked his location and found he was allegedly at yet another massage parlor.
Clery spoke about how she found out her husband was allegedly unfaithful. (Laura Clery)

"If I could say anything to my then-self, I’d tell her to buckle up," Clery wrote. "Change the locks. Call your mom, call your lawyer, call your best friend. Believe the voice inside your head when it tells you that something is wrong. Be smart, be brave, and you’ll get through this."

The following day, Clery recalled a family trip to Malibu, during which Hilton allegedly began screaming in front of their young children that he planned to take his life. She alleged that he screamed "I’m going to kill myself, and it’s your f---ing fault!" He then left the house and Clery called the police, but once they found him, he presented as "a man who was absolutely fine—a man with a crazy, overdramatic wife."
Clery said her ex-husband once allegedly threatened to kill himself in front of their children during a family outing. (Stewart Cook/Getty Images for Apple TV+)

She claims that she woke up the next day to messages asking if she was OK, and discovered Hilton had taken to social media and shared details of the incident with his followers. She says he allegedly didn't seem to care that she was upset about his videos, helping her realize he didn't care about salvaging their relationship, and that they needed time apart. She also alleged she later found out that Hilton had relapsed in his drug addiction at this time.

"I realized in a flash of clarity—truly, it felt like life b-----slapping me in the face—that I had deluded myself into thinking that the worst was over," she wrote. "I knew in my bones that we were a ways from better days. We had to separate."
From there, Clery writes that the separation evolved into years of legal disputes, financial hardship and a painful process of rebuilding her life as a single mother.

Clery alleges Hilton later broke into her home, leading to his arrest, hacked her social media accounts and launched an online community that portrayed her as Satan, claims she says further damaged both her finances and emotional well-being.
Clery struggled financially during her separation and divorce. (David Livingston/Getty Images)

The couple announced their separation in August 2022 and filed for divorce in June 2023. In the memoir, Clery also goes into detail about her financial struggles following their separation and divorce.

She recalled staying in mediation with Hilton for too long, because she "was scared to let go of my creative partner" and "scared to stop sharing the bills with him," but also thought that by continuing to work with him, she could help him, but noted, "You can’t pay your water bill with good intentions."

"That fear cost me two years and so much money," she wrote. "Thousands and thousands of dollars gone, until I didn’t have the money left to even keep the endless mediation going. Maybe that was Stephen’s plan all along. Maybe he wanted me to bleed out financially. And maybe I played right into it."
JAMIE-LYNN SIGLER CLAIMS HER EX-HUSBAND SECRETLY STOLE HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS FROM HER 'SOPRANOS' EARNINGS
Clery described "living from massive paycheck to massive paycheck," claiming she was paying both her mortgage and Hilton's mortgage, along with two years of mediation.
Clery said she was left broke after paying for her estranged husband's mortgage and mediation for a number of years. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images for dick clark productions)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
She explained that during their marriage "Stephen handled the money," and after her water was shut off one evening, she "realized I had handed away my power with every bill I refused to look at."

"My water got shut off. In my three-million-dollar house. Yes, you read that correctly. I was broke. In a three-million-dollar house," she wrote. "Having my water shut off? Yeah, that was my bottom. But it was a lesson I needed to learn. Look at the d--- bills. Face the scary thing. Because if you keep ignoring it, you’ll get something much scarier than dry taps and overflowing toilets."

In the midst of their separation, Clery endured false allegations against her that she abused her children, but ultimately was awarded full custody, with Hilton getting supervised visitation, but she is hopeful about his recovery.
Clery was awarded full custody, but is hopeful her ex-husband will recover. (Mike McGinnis/Getty Images)

"One day, maybe, Alfie and Poppy will be able to spend time with their dad without court supervision. Maybe Stephen will stay sober. To his credit, by mid-November, he passed one hundred days of sobriety. Maybe this chapter of our lives might finally be coming to a close. Maybe. Time will tell," she concluded. "For now, my guard is up, my boundaries are firm, and I’m cautiously inching toward hope again."
Hilton has publicly discussed his struggles with addiction and his mental health in the years since their separation.

title: Sean Penn reveals chilling thought after finding himself alone with the 'Night Stalker' in jail
summary: Sean Penn reveals he was shackled just feet from serial killer Richard Ramirez in Los Angeles County Jail and briefly considered attacking the "Night Stalker."
story: Actor Sean Penn joins Hannity to discuss his view of the Russian invasion and his new picture, which began filming prior to the conflict.
Sean Penn admits he briefly considered attacking one of America's most infamous serial killers after the two unexpectedly came face to face behind bars.

In a recent interview with VICE News, the actor recalled spending 34 days in Los Angeles County Jail during the height of his early Hollywood success. Penn said he was in his mid-20s, had already starred in "Taps" and filmed "Colors," and was married to Madonna when he crossed paths with the "Night Stalker."

"I got moved out of general population because of some kind of threat," the 65-year-old told the outlet. "... And a lot of guys on this department... they invest a lot in pretending not to give a s--- about Hollywood culture, but they sure do like to gossip [about] what they see."
LISA RINNA REVEALS HOW HER MOTHER SURVIVED BRUTAL HAMMER ATTACK BY NOTORIOUS ‘TRAILSIDE KILLER’

Sean Penn, left, told VICE News he was just 24 or 25 when he spent 34 days in Los Angeles County Jail and unexpectedly crossed paths with serial killer Richard Ramirez, right. (Stephane Cardinale/Corbis via Getty Images; Getty Images)

"So, I slept with one eye open, of course," he said. "... Then I got moved to [an] eight and a half by 11 by myself for most of the time. And through a little wire glass door, there's Richard Ramirez, not 20 feet away. And we're both insomniacs."
Shackled and belly chained for a phone call, the actor said he was escorted into an otherwise empty room — only to discover Ramirez sitting beside him.
WATCH: SEAN PENN DISCUSSES DOCUMENTARY ON UKRAINE WAR

"I came out of my cell for a phone call," Penn told the outlet. "So they take you shackled and belly chained, and they take one cuff off, put it on the eye hook so that you've got a hand for the phone. And Ramirez is seated right next to me. He's going to [make] a call also."
Richard Ramirez is seen in court on Oct. 9, 1985, in Los Angeles. (Getty Images)

"There's nobody else there," said Penn. "There's nobody in there because somebody was throwing feces at somebody. It was a crazy kind of thing happening. And I did have that question. I knew what he did to some of these people. This wasn't today's phones or your cellphone, right?"
"I'm right next to him," said Penn. "I could, I could ..."
"Flatten him out," said the host.
Sean Penn opened up about spending 34 days near serial killer Richard Ramirez — and the split-second temptation he says he had during their face-to-face encounter. (Marc Piasecki/Getty Images)
The Oscar winner admitted he thought better of it despite having access to him "twice."
"But who was I?" said Penn. "It was just another person. And I'm so glad I didn't think I was important enough to do that, but you have the thought."
Ramirez was convicted of 13 murders during a killing spree that gripped Southern California in 1984 and 1985.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Richard Ramirez received the death penalty in 1989 after being convicted of 13 murders and numerous other violent crimes. (Bettmann Archive)

His reign of terror peaked in the summer of 1985, when he slipped into homes through unlocked doors and windows before murdering victims, sexually assaulting women and burglarizing homes. He also left satanic symbols at several crime scenes.
The press dubbed him the "Night Stalker" as authorities warned Southern California residents to lock their doors and windows after dark.

Ramirez's slayings ended in 1985 after residents of an East Los Angeles neighborhood recognized him from news reports, chased him down and beat him before police took him into custody following a failed carjacking.
Richard Ramirez is seen here flashing the "devil's horn" sign before shouting "evil" to reporters. (Bettmann Archive)
During his trial, the Texas native attracted a following of young women who regularly attended court proceedings and sent him love letters.
Ramirez died in 2013 at age 53 from cancer while awaiting execution on California's death row at San Quentin State Prison.

Years before, Penn revealed another bizarre detail about their time behind bars: The serial killer wanted his autograph. Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter in 2015, Penn said Ramirez sent word through a deputy requesting a signed keepsake.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Sean Penn attends the "Into the Wild" By Sean Penn event during the 17th Film Festival Lumiere on Oct. 12, 2025, in Lyon, France. (WireImage)

"He wrote me [a letter]," said Penn. "I was down here on Bauchet Street, in LA County Jail, in the cell kind of across from him. And after a month of seeing each other around, he wanted my autograph. So, he sent one of the deputies over, [and the] deputy came to my cell and told me, ‘Hey, Richard Ramirez wants your autograph.’ And I didn’t trust the deputy because I’d gotten in some trouble inside there and just passing a piece of paper is contraband, so you can get extra days for that, and I already had extra days and I didn’t want more."
Sean Penn told VICE News he was already married to Madonna when his encounter with Richard Ramirez occurred. (Getty Images)

"So, I said, ‘Bring the sergeant down here, and I’ll talk to him, and if he approves it, then I want him to write something first, and I’ll write him something back,’" said Penn. "So, the sergeant came down and approved it, and they went over to Ramirez — this guard basically wanted to play cupid, in some way. So, I get this thing from him, and it says, ‘Hey Sean, stay tough and hit them again — Richard Ramirez, 666,’ with a pentagram and a rendition of the devil."
Penn wrote back.
Sean Penn told The Hollywood Reporter what happened to the handwritten note he received from Richard Ramirez. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

"I said, ‘You know, Richard, it’s impossible to be incarcerated and not feel a certain kinship with your fellow inmates. Well, Richard, I’ve done the impossible. I feel absolutely no kinship with you. And I hope gas descends upon you before sanity does, you know? It would be a kinder way out.’"
"And they gave it to him," said Penn. "And then my house burned down years later, and that damn thing of his burned with it."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Cole Hauser admits Taylor Sheridan's absence from writers' room created 'challenges' on 'Dutton Ranch'
summary: The "Yellowstone" actor admitted "everything had changed" on "Dutton Ranch" after Taylor Sheridan stepped back, saying the cast had to "figure out" a new creative team.
story: The "Dutton Ranch" star reflects on his family’s deep ties to Montana as the Paramount+ series premieres May 15 with two episodes, followed by weekly releases.
Cole Hauser is giving fans a glimpse behind the scenes of "Dutton Ranch" — and it wasn't all smooth riding.

The actor, who reprises his fan-favorite role as Rip Wheeler in the "Yellowstone" spin-off, acknowledged the cast faced an uphill battle after franchise creator Taylor Sheridan stepped away from the show's writers' room during the spin-off’s first season.

"There were challenges, you know?" Hauser told Film Inside NYC. "Not having Taylor [Sheridan] there, for us to really kind of be able to work with these new writers, these new directors, these people... Everything had changed."
ED HARRIS SAYS HE WAS READY TO LEAVE DUTTON RANCH AFTER FEELING MISLED ABOUT HIS ROLE
Cole Hauser previously said his "Dutton Ranch" character Rip Wheeler reflects a "throwback to the old-school American man." (John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images; Lauren "Lo" Smith/Paramount+)
"The only… normality that we had whatsoever was Carter [played by Finn Little], Christina [director Alexandra Voros] … Kelly and myself," he added.
"Dutton Ranch," which wrapped its first season earlier this month, marked the first series in the "Yellowstone" universe not to be written by Sheridan.
While the franchise creator remained on board as an executive producer, day-to-day creative duties shifted to showrunner Chad Feehan and an entirely new writing staff.
For Hauser, the transition wasn't seamless.

"I enjoy a challenge, it certainly was a challenge," he said. "We worked our a--es off this year... And I don't think a lot of the outside noise or the thought of, like, 'What's the weight of the show?' was really apparent to me at the time."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Kelly Reilly as Beth Dutton and Cole Hauser as Rip Wheeler in "Dutton Ranch." (Emerson Miller/Paramount+.)
Rather than dwell on the expectations surrounding one of television's biggest franchises, Hauser said the cast focused on finding its footing with an unfamiliar creative team.
The actor pointed out that the experience ultimately strengthened the cast.
TAYLOR SHERIDAN’S 'YELLOWSTONE’ FORMULA TURNS COUNTRY STARS INTO SCENE-STEALERS AS MORGAN WADE MAKES HER DEBUT
Cole Hauser reveals the "Dutton Ranch" cast had to adapt after Taylor Sheridan stepped back. (Omar Vega/Getty Images)

"It was about putting my head down and working my a-- off with… what I had around me. The writers that we had, the new writers that we had, that we had to figure out on our feet how to really perform and tell a story. So, I'm proud of what we accomplished, and I look forward to doing it again."
Hauser's comments come after speculation surrounding the show's creative direction.

Ed Harris previously said he told his team to get him out of "Dutton Ranch." (Emerson Miller/Paramount+.)

Speaking to Variety, Harris said, "Midway through this first season, I was ready to say, 'Get me the f--- out of here,' to tell you the truth... I didn't feel I was being used... I felt a little bit misled."
Harris claimed he signed on believing Everett would be one of the show's central characters, but felt that promise never materialized.

title: William Shatner and daughter Melanie reveal they battled Stage 4 cancer at the same time
summary: Melanie Shatner Gretsch reveals how a late-night lump led to her HER2-positive breast cancer diagnosis while her father faced Stage 4 melanoma.
story: Shatner told Fox News Digital it's only natural to focus on different things at different stages in life.
William Shatner and his 61-year-old daughter revealed this week that the two of them battled cancer at the same time several years ago.
Melanie Shatner Gretsch first discovered her cancer four years ago when she woke up in the middle of the night and felt a little lump on her breast she thought might be a bug bite.
She told People magazine she decided to have it checked out despite a mammogram not finding anything just five months earlier.
DAVE COULIER REVEALS 45-POUND WEIGHT LOSS, GRUELING SIDE EFFECTS FROM CANCER FIGHTS
William Shatner with his daughter, Melanie Shatner; her husband, Joel Gretsch; and their daughter, Willow, in 2006. (Barry King/WireImage)

Although the technician didn’t find anything during a scan the next day, "something pushed me back and said, ‘No, have her recheck it.’ She put the wand exactly where I put my finger and under her breath said, ‘Now, I would have missed that.’"
She was diagnosed with HER2-positive breast cancer that had spread to lymph nodes in her chest.
Shatner said his daughter was "very conscious of the importance of her life for herself and for her family. I was devastated."
Gretsch is a mother to two daughters she shares with husband Joel Gretsch.
Gretsch said her father told her not to worry about the medical costs and to send him the bills.
"Then you made me laugh so hard when I was still going to the doctor a year later," she added. "You said, ‘You’ve got to get well. We’re going to be in the poorhouse.’"
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
William Shatner at MegaCon Orlando 2026 in March. (Getty Images)
For the next 18 months, her life was filled with multiple rounds of chemo, 30 radiation treatments and a double mastectomy.
"Chemo was the most physically draining, and the radiation I found so emotionally draining," she admitted.
Just as she was nearing the end of her treatments, a lump appeared on her dad’s cheek.

He said a family doctor told him it was just a blocked salivary gland that was nothing to worry about, but a doctor friend whose advice he asked while they were horseback riding advised him to get it removed.
CAMERON MATHISON SAYS NOTICING SUBTLE BODY CHANGES ‘SAVED MY LIFE’ AFTER CANCER DIAGNOSIS
"He placed his hands on my cheeks, and he said with love in his voice, ‘You better get this out,’" Shatner explained.
In June 2023, Shatner was diagnosed with Stage 4 malignant melanoma that had spread to his lungs and brain.
"I remember vividly thinking, ‘I don’t have the strength to take care of myself and lose my father at the same time,’" Gretsch admitted.
Shatner was more upbeat.
"They said, ‘You got cancer. If you came in later, you would have been dead.’ See? That’s my life. I think the universe is taking care of me."
The 95-year-old had the tumor removed and underwent two years of immunotherapy.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"He wouldn’t stop his life," his daughter told People magazine. "He kept working and moving forward. Whenever he was home, Joel and I would bring dinner to him and watch movies, just always made sure that he’s not alone."
William Shatner on "Star Trek" (Bettmann Archive)
Shatner added, "We got the perfect doctors for her cancer and my cancer."
The "Star Trek" actor, who was the oldest man in space when he went up in a Blue Origin rocket, has stayed busy with two new books and two records, all expected to come out next year.
"I’m healthier now than I’ve been in years," Shatner said. "The brain is like a muscle. It feeds on activity."
Near the end of 2024, both were declared cancer free.
"It was the third time in my life I had heard him cry," Gretsch admitted of telling him her cancer was gone.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Shatner said the experience has given him a new perspective on life.
"I’m thinking of the miracle of a hummingbird, and of my dog taking a ball and my children," he said. "I’m aware of the magic of it all."
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Jason Alexander apologizes after Courtney Stodden says 2012 comedy sketch objectified her as a minor
summary: Jason Alexander apologized to Courtney Stodden after she shared a photo from a 2012 sketch where he rubbed a cellphone across her chest when she was 17.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Jason Alexander is taking accountability for his past mistakes.

The 66-year-old actor recently apologized to Courtney Stodden for participating in a 2012 Funny or Die sketch in which he held a cellphone up to her chest and made comments about her body when she was a minor.

"Looking back at the comedy sketch in which Ms. Stodden and I participated in 2012, I completely agree that it was inappropriate and I truly regret it," he told Fox News Digital in a statement. "But more importantly, I am deeply sorry for any harm or distress it has caused Ms. Stodden. I offer her my sincerest apologies."
His apology comes one day after Stodden called out Alexander on Instagram as one of the writers of the sketch, adding, "As an adult, that fact has become harder—not easier—for me to understand."
GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'
Alexander apologized to Stodden for a 2012 sketch in which he objectified her body. (Getty Images)
In the Instagram post, she shared a photo of her and Alexander in the sketch, in which she is wearing a bikini, and the actor is rubbing a cellphone across her chest.

"I was 17 years old in this photo. The older I get, the more impossible this is to understand," she wrote. "During this comedy sketch, Jason Alexander repeatedly rubbed his phone across my breasts while saying there was 'no signal' in my head but 'plenty of signal' in my chest. Later in the sketch, he joked that when I turned 18 he’d like to take me behind the couch and 'have his way' with me."
She added that as a minor she "didn’t have the legal power to decide whether I wanted to participate" and that "the contracts were signed by adults."
At the time, she was married to Doug Hutchison, who she tied the knot with when she was 16 and he was 51, noting the paycheck for this appearance went to him.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Stodden described feeling alone while on the set of Funny or Die. (Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty Images)

"I was the only child in the room. I felt so alone," she added. "Looking back now, I don’t see comedy. I see a 17-year-old girl whose body became part of an adult joke. People still say, 'You chose to be there.' Legally, I couldn’t make those decisions for myself. That’s the point."
She ended the post by acknowledging that while she isn't able to change what she went through, she finds herself asking, "How did so many adults look at a minor and decide this was acceptable?"
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
"That’s exactly why I speak out today," she concluded. "Children deserve laws that protect them. They shouldn’t have to become adults before realizing the law should have protected them all along."

The caption also included a call to support California Assembly Bill 1267, which aims to permanently end child marriage by setting the minimum legal age for marriage in California to 18 with no exceptions.
Stodden married Hutchison when she was 16 and he was 51, and is now advocating for legislation banning child marriage without exception. (JB Lacroix/WireImage)

Stodden and Hutchison got married in 2011 despite their 34-year age gap. They split up and got back together a few times before officially calling it quits in 2016, although divorce papers were not filed until March 2018, with the divorce being finalized in March 2020.
She announced their divorce in an Instagram post featuring her wedding photo, calling it "an emotional day," but assured her fans "it’s for the better."
Stodden announced her divorce on Instagram in March 2020, saying in the caption she now feels taken advantage of. (Tibrina Hobson/Getty Images)

"I look back at this picture and feel absolutely taken advantage of," she wrote. "I’ve been scared to even speak up about feeling groomed or being verbally abused during the almost 10 year marriage because I was a child and he was 50 when we married but I’m a woman now and it’s time for me to put my big girl pants on and speak on this matter."
She continued: "I’ve felt completely trapped, manipulated and at times abandoned by adults // growing up in such an environment — it became a lonely and dark place."

title: 'Dutton Ranch' star Ed Harris blasts producers, says he wanted to void contract: 'Get me the f--- out'
summary: Ed Harris says he felt "misled" about his role in "Dutton Ranch" and told his team to get him out before production wrapped on the first season.
story: The "Dutton Ranch" star reflects on his family’s deep ties to Montana as the Paramount+ series premieres May 15 with two episodes, followed by weekly releases.
Ed Harris says he came close to walking away from Taylor Sheridan's "Dutton Ranch."
The veteran actor revealed he felt "underused and inconsequential" while filming the show's first season, prompting him to tell his team to "get me the f--- out of here" before production wrapped.

"Prior to signing on for it, I was talked to quite a bit about what the season was, and what my character was going to do — and that I was one of the four main characters," Harris told Variety. "And that wasn't really the case."
COLE HAUSER SAYS HIS FAMILY HELPED SHAPE MONTANA AS FANS FOLLOW TAYLOR SHERIDAN FROM TREASURE STATE TO TEXAS
Ed Harris says he nearly quit Taylor Sheridan's "Dutton Ranch." (Emerson Miller/Paramount+.)

title: Angelina Jolie achieves 'complete cutting of ties' between kids and Brad Pitt as twins turn 18: expert
summary: Five of Brad Pitt's children have dropped his surname as a family law expert says Angelina Jolie achieved the "complete cutting of ties" she sought.
story: Jon Voight spoke to Fox News Digital while promoting his film "Reagan," and weighed in on the family drama between his daughter Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt.
A decade after one of Hollywood's most bitter divorces began, Angelina Jolie has finally achieved a "complete cutting of ties" with ex-husband Brad Pitt.

With the former couple's youngest children now 18, the last legal thread connecting Jolie and Pitt has effectively been severed, a family law expert explained to Fox News Digital. The expert argued the Oscar winner has reached the outcome she had been seeking since filing for divorce in 2016.

"For those that followed the Pitt/Jolie divorce since 2016, it should be no surprise that Angelina Jolie is finally able to achieve what she attempted to get in the 2016 divorce — a complete cutting of ties between the children and Brad Pitt," Holly Davis, cofounder of Kirker Davis LLP, told Fox News Digital.
BRAD PITT FACES FRESH FAMILY BLOW AS DAUGHTER CLEARS MAJOR HURDLE TO DROP HIS LAST NAME

Angelina Jolie has achieved what one family law expert described as a "complete cutting of ties" between ex-husband Brad Pitt and their kids after the former couple's youngest children turned 18. (Toni Anne Barson Archive/WireImage)
Pitt and Jolie share six children: Maddox, Zahara, Shiloh, Pax, Knox and Vivienne.
Twins Knox and Vivienne reaching adulthood on July 12 means custody issues are no longer before the court, giving Jolie the freedom to make decisions that previously required court oversight.

"Because she was unable to achieve this result in the parties' divorce, she had to wait until the youngest children were 18 to be able to do the things that the court would not allow her to do," Davis explained.
What ultimately drove the children's estrangement from their father remains impossible to know from the outside, according to Davis.

"Whether or not she influenced them in hating their father based on the legitimate problems in her romantic relationship with Brad, or whether they all suffered similar difficult moments as a family which lead to their decision to no longer see him, will be anyone's guess," the family attorney said.

Jolie and Pitt's daughter Vivienne is seeking to remove "Pitt" legally from her last name — from Vivienne Marcheline Jolie-Pitt to Vivienne Marcheline Jolie — just over a week after turning 18, according to People magazine.
The petition was filed in Los Angeles County Superior Court, with the reason for the name change noted as "personal," per the outlet, with the hearing scheduled for November 2.

Two years prior, Vivienne worked on the Broadway play "The Outsiders" with mom Angelina, and was credited as "Vivienne Jolie" in the playbill. Vivienne worked as a producer assistant on the musical while Angelina served as a producer.
Family law and entertainment experts are divided over whether Brad Pitt's strained relationship with several of his children will have any lasting impact on the actor's public image. (Getty Images)
BRAD PITT FIGHTS FOR SURVIVAL IN 'HEART OF THE BEAST' TRAILER AS FANS SAY HE'S 'COOLER' THAN YOUNGER ACTORS
Jolie may have effectively severed the remaining legal family ties, but experts say the public fallout might not significantly damage Pitt's Hollywood standing.

"Brandwise, it’s not that big of a hit to Brad Pitt’s name or brand," entertainment attorney Tre Lovell told Fox News Digital. "He’s such a universally well-known star, and his divorce with Angelina Jolie and strained relationship with his kids have been well publicized."

"Most of the public would chalk it up to an unfortunate problem with the relationship with his kids, but as far as his brand, it’s still strong and would survive any type of criticism in this area," the lawyer for Los Angeles-based Lovell Firm explained.

Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie's yearslong family divide has entered a new chapter as legal experts weigh in on what their twins reaching adulthood means for the former couple. (Jason LaVeris/FilmMagic via Getty)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Five of Pitt and Jolie's children have distanced themselves from the actor by dropping his surname, with Vivienne and three of her siblings choosing to make the change official legally.

"[Pitt's] talent remains unquestioned. But when multiple adult children publicly choose to stop using your surname, the conversation inevitably shifts from career to character," crisis communications expert Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital. "Whether fair or unfair, that’s the kind of narrative no amount of good publicity can easily overcome."
Four of Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt's kids have made moves to legally drop the actor's surname. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

Zahara filed to formally remove "Pitt" from her surname in June. If granted, her legal name will change from Zahara Marley Jolie-Pitt to Zahara Marley Jolie. Her name change follows Shiloh's name change in 2024. Maddox also reportedly filed a petition in May.

"This isn’t about a single family decision… it’s about accumulation," he added. "One child dropping a famous last name might be dismissed as an isolated event. When it happens repeatedly across multiple adult children, it stops looking like celebrity gossip and starts becoming part of a public figure’s legacy."
Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt finalized their divorce in 2024, but experts say the former couple's highly public family conflict continues to generate headlines. (STR/AFP via Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Experts told Fox News Digital that Brad Pitt's Hollywood brand remains strong despite renewed attention on his relationship with his children and ex-wife Angelina Jolie. (Getty Images)

The public's reaction to the family drama, however, remains open to interpretation. While some experts believe the repeated rejection of Pitt's surname could become part of his public legacy, others contend the developments may instead generate sympathy for the Oscar-winning actor.

"One of the primary things that parents should focus on in a divorce is the well-being of the child, and that often means striving for the child to have a healthy relationship with both parents," Jordan Matthews told Fox News Digital.

The entertainment attorney for Los Angeles-based Holtz Matthews LLP argued that while the decision to drop Pitt's last name was "highly personal," it is likely to leave many members of the public "sympathetic to Pitt’s position."

title: Measles surge hits new milestone as US cases surpass last year's total
summary: U.S. measles cases in 2026 have officially surpassed 2025 totals, with 93% of patients unvaccinated or unknown for MMR as outbreaks persist.
story: Dr. Nicole Saphier discusses the significant measles outbreak in Spartanburg County, South Carolina, with declining vaccination rates across the U.S.
Measles has reemerged as a persistent public health challenge in the U.S. over the past two years — and the spread isn't slowing down.
According to a Johns Hopkins University tracker that compiles local and state health data, there were 2,295 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. as of July 22.
This figure has officially surpassed the 2025 numbers, which totaled 2,286 measles cases nationwide.
MEASLES-INFECTED TRAVELER MAY HAVE EXPOSED PASSENGERS AT LAX AND NEARBY HOTEL, HEALTH OFFICIALS WARN
Cases have been reported across the country, but concentrated outbreaks have worsened in some areas of Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Florida, Virginia, Utah, Texas and Arizona.
In 2025, Texas had the largest outbreak — totaling 803 cases throughout the state.
Measles cases have officially surpassed 2025 numbers, which totaled 2,286 cases. The U.S. has reported 2,295 measles cases so far in 2026. (iStock)

In the latest CDC measles update on July 17, there were 34 new outbreaks reported in 2026, compared to 48 outbreaks in 2025. Most cases were associated with local outbreaks, while some were linked to international visitors.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Both this year and last year, 93% of all measles patients were either unvaccinated for measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), or had an unknown vaccination status, data shows.
Most cases have occurred in children and young adults between the ages of 5 and 19.
There have been no deaths reported in 2026, according to the CDC, but there were three deaths in 2025.

Most cases have occurred in children and young adults between the ages of 5 and 19. There have been no deaths reported in 2026, according to the CDC, but there were three deaths in 2025. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
The rise in cases comes more than two decades after health agencies reported that the disease was eliminated in 2000.

Measles can be spread through direct contact with infectious droplets, or can be airborne when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes, according to health officials. The virus can remain infectious in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Symptoms usually appear within a week or two, and may include a high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes.
A few days later, flat, red spots appear on the face and then spread down the neck to the rest of the body. People are most contagious in the four days before and four days after the rash appears.
Community protection
Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, emphasized the highly contagious nature of measles.

"Measles is so contagious that up to 90% of susceptible people who are exposed to an infected person will become infected," he told Fox News Digital, noting the importance of community protection. "We need a 95% vaccine coverage rate to ensure herd immunity," he said.
A paramedic administers a dose of the measles vaccine at a health center in Lubbock, Texas, on Feb. 27, 2025. (RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP via Getty Images)
The herd immunity threshold is a mathematical estimate based on how contagious a disease is and how effectively immunity from vaccination or prior infection prevents its spread, according to Siegel.

"In this case, two-dose vaccination is almost 100% effective, and natural immunity after a measles infection is generally lifelong," the doctor said. "This isn’t about personal choice, it’s about community protection. We need to protect those who can’t have a live virus vaccine because they are immunocompromised or pregnant."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The doctor also cautioned that the U.S. could be at risk of losing its measles elimination status, as the number and duration of outbreaks suggest sustained local transmission within the U.S., rather than isolated cases linked only to international travel.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The CDC recommends that everyone receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, calling vaccination the best protection against measles.
Anyone who is showing measles symptoms or thinks they’ve been exposed should self-isolate and contact their doctor before showing up to a medical center and infecting others.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Sharon Stone's terrifying weed withdrawal sparks warning about today's potent marijuana
summary: Sharon Stone's marijuana withdrawal symptoms were so severe that she saw a neurologist, highlighting the dangers of quitting high-potency THC without a plan.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses new research that casts doubt on cannabis benefits and highlights increased mental health risks, especially for teenagers. Modern marijuana, with 70-90% THC potency, is linked to higher rates of PTSD, anxiety, depression, ADHD, and bipolar disorder. Usage among Americans aged 12 and older has skyrocketed by 180% since the early 2000s, leading to concerns about addiction and health issues.
Hollywood icon Sharon Stone recently opened up about a health scare after quitting marijuana, revealing her symptoms were so intense that she turned to a neurologist.
During an interview with Variety, the actress said her decision to quit was driven by a desire for a drug-free life.
"And because I think they put so much stuff in it now — they really do — when I stopped smoking pot, I also got sick," she said.
CANNABIS COMPOUNDS COULD REVERSE DISEASE AFFECTING ONE-THIRD OF ADULTS
"I got pretty sick for a month. I went to my neurologist, and he said, ‘Sharon, I’ve had people dying in the emergency room from marijuana.'"
Stone attributed her ordeal to the potency of modern weed, saying, "It’s not like you’re pulling it out of the ground anymore ... It’s not like when we were kids."
American actress Sharon Stone quit "smoking pot" and got so sick that she consulted a neurologist, she revealed in a recent interview. (Getty Images, iStock)

Experts note that cannabis withdrawal itself is generally not considered life-threatening, although severe symptoms, underlying medical conditions or interactions with other substances can complicate recovery.
FLYING WITH CANNABIS? TSA'S NEW GUIDANCE COMES WITH A MAJOR HEALTH WARNING
Dr. Chris Tuell, clinical director of addiction services at the Lindner Center in Cincinnati, confirmed that today's cannabis products are vastly different from the strains of decades past.
THC levels in marijuana have surged from about 3% to 5% in the 1980s to as high as 30% in today's cannabis products, while concentrates can exceed 90% THC, he told Fox News Digital.
"I do believe cannabis is addicting, especially with the high levels of THC."

Higher THC concentrations have been linked to greater risks of dependence, cannabis use disorder (CUD), psychosis in some users and more severe withdrawal symptoms, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse.

As today's cannabis products become increasingly potent, experts say there are several risks and warning signs that daily users should know before deciding whether to continue — or quit — using marijuana.
No. 1: High-potency THC changes the brain's reward system
According to Cleveland Clinic, CUD occurs when marijuana takes over the brain's reward pathways, amplifying compulsive behavior.
"I do believe cannabis is addicting, especially with the high levels of THC," Tuell told Fox News Digital.
No. 2: Addiction isn't always obvious

The American Psychiatric Association’s DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition) outlines the following diagnostic criteria signaling that casual use may have crossed into dependency.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Taking larger amounts over longer periods than intendedExperiencing unsuccessful attempts to cut down or control usageFailing to fulfill work, school or home responsibilitiesContinuing use despite clear relationship problems
Taking larger amounts over longer periods than intended
Experiencing unsuccessful attempts to cut down or control usage
Failing to fulfill work, school or home responsibilities
Continuing use despite clear relationship problems
Today’s cannabis flower and concentrates contain up to 90% THC, making modern products exponentially stronger than those from decades past, experts say. (iStock)
No. 3: Withdrawal can be intense
Quitting heavy, long-term cannabis use can trigger withdrawal symptoms within 24 to 48 hours, Cleveland Clinic notes.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Users frequently experience severe insomnia, intense irritability, anxiety, appetite loss, sweating, headaches and stomach upset. While acute physical symptoms typically resolve within a month, mood swings and sleep issues can linger much longer, according to Tuell.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
4. Medical guidance may be needed

While cannabis withdrawal alone rarely requires hospitalization, Cleveland Clinic notes that people with significant medical or mental health conditions — or those stopping cannabis while also withdrawing from alcohol, opioids or certain other medications — may benefit from medical supervision.
Addiction experts strongly advise stepping down THC intake slowly to cushion the impact on the nervous system and avoid severe rebound symptoms. (iStock)
No. 5: Underlying issues may fuel dependence

Mental health conditions often occur alongside cannabis use disorder, and treating those underlying issues may help reduce problematic marijuana use, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Cleveland Clinic.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"I strongly believe that CUD and mental health issues co-exist, and that mental health counseling can address the issues driving the addictive behaviors," Tuell said.
Fox News Digital reached out to Stone's representatives requesting comment.

title: Microplastics detected in most heart attack patients' blood in startling new study
summary: Nearly 84% of severe heart attack patients had detectable microplastics in their coronary artery blood, with polyethylene found in 97% of cases.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel sits down with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin for an exclusive interview on a new push to remove microplastics from the food supply and environment.

Patients experiencing severe heart attacks may have significantly higher concentrations of micro- and nanoplastics in their blood compared to individuals with stable heart conditions, according to new research.
Italian researchers analyzed blood samples from the coronary arteries of 61 patients undergoing angiograms, a procedure that analyzes blood vessels for irregularities.

They found that nearly 84% of patients suffering an active, severe heart attack had detectable micro- and nanoplastics in their blood. In contrast, plastic was detected in 40% of patients with chronic heart disease and only 32% of those with normal coronary arteries.
NOTABLE FIGURES WHO DIED FROM THE SAME HEART CONDITION LINKED TO LINDSEY GRAHAM'S DEATH
Researchers led by Dr. Raffaele Marfella of the University of Campania Luigi Vanvitelli in Naples conducted the study, which was published in the European Heart Journal.
Polyethylene, a common material used in plastic bags and bottles, appeared in 97% of those patients who tested positive.
Severe heart attack patients were significantly more likely to have micro- and nanoplastics in their blood than those with stable heart conditions or clear arteries. (iStock)

"This study adds to emerging research showing the potential role of micro- and nanoplastics in heart disease," Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished.com, told Fox News Digital.
While notable, the findings should be considered in the broader context of environmental health hazards, said New York City-based Routhenstein, who was not involved in the study.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

"While these findings are interesting and highlight the importance of paying attention to environmental factors that may contribute to inflammation and blood vessel injury, they do not prove that plastics cause heart attacks," she said.
The findings align with previous research detecting microplastics in arterial plaque, Routhenstein noted, although she cautioned that the study has several limitations.
A history of smoking emerged as the single strongest predictor of detectable plastic particles in the blood, the researchers found. (iStock)

"This was an observational study, so it can only show an association, not cause and effect," she said. "It also included a relatively small group of patients from one country, so we can't assume the findings apply to everyone."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Health and environmental variables could also complicate the data. In the study, a history of smoking emerged as the single strongest predictor of detectable plastic particles in the blood.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Factors like smoking and air pollution are also linked to cardiovascular disease and higher plastic exposure, making it difficult to separate the independent effects of microplastics," Routhenstein said.
Heating food in glass or ceramic instead of plastic is one way to reduce exposure to microplastics, according to experts. (iStock)
To reduce potential risk, the dietitian recommends making targeted swaps to help limit daily exposure to microplastics.

"I would take inventory of your regular sources of microplastic exposure and see where you can reduce or swap them for better alternatives," Routhenstein said. "For example, replace plastic food storage containers with glass ones."
She also urged taking extra precautions when preparing meals and drinking water.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"When microwaving or reheating food, use glass or ceramic containers instead of plastic," she said. "It's also a good idea to limit plastic water bottles and single-use plastic containers, especially when they're exposed to heat."
She added, "Think of reducing plastic exposure as one piece of an overall heart-healthy lifestyle."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Men switched at birth uncover hospital mix-up after DNA test decades later
summary: A DNA test gift revealed Kyle Bylin had no genetic match to his family, leading to the discovery he and Jeremy Morrison were switched at birth in 1988.
story: Jeremy Morrison and Kyle Bylin, born in 1988, share their story after a DNA test revealed they were switched at birth nearly 40 years ago. The men are now suing Unity Medical Center in North Dakota for answers, as the hospital claims no existing records from that time. This extraordinary case highlights the emotional impact of such a mix-up.

Two North Dakota men are suing a local hospital after discovering they were switched at birth nearly four decades ago, a revelation brought to light by a surprise result from a direct-to-consumer genetic test.
The men joined Fox & Friends on Thursday to discuss their journey.

The mix-up was uncovered two years ago when Kyle Bylin received an at-home DNA test as a gift. Bylin says he was shocked when the results showed no genetic match to anyone in the family that raised him.
TWO FAMILIES SUE NORTH DAKOTA HOSPITAL ON ALLEGATIONS BABIES WERE SWITCHED AT BIRTH
"It was absolutely mind-blowing," Bylin told Fox & Friends. "We knew the DNA trail didn’t make sense, but to find out you’ve been switched at birth is a huge revelation."

Instead, the data pointed to a biological aunt, leading Bylin to her nephew, Jeremy Morrison. Subsequent DNA testing confirmed that Morrison and Bylin had been raised by each other’s biological families.
"[My parents] will always be my parents. A DNA test isn’t going to change 38 years of memories overnight," Morrison said.
Kyle Bylin and Jeremy Morrison were the only two babies born at Unity Medical Center in Grafton, North Dakota, on Jan. 26, 1988, the lawsuit says. (Google Maps)
Morrison recalled having long-standing doubts while growing up, noting that he often made light of the physical differences between himself and the woman who raised him.
MELINDA FRENCH GATES SAYS IT TOOK 3 DOCTORS TO DIAGNOSE THE CONDITION SHE WAS SUFFERING FROM
"I kind of had a feeling inside that I was adopted or, you know, she stole me or something like that," Morrison said. But that doesn’t necessarily mean he’d change what happened, he added.
"It’s a little bit of nature, a little bit of nurture, and you end up with the life that you have," he said when asked if he’d go back and undo the switch.
SISTERS IN VIRAL VIDEO REVEAL TRUTH OF 'EERIE' FAMILY PHOTO THEY DISCOVERED AT RENTAL HOME
The emotional toll of the discovery has weighed heavily on both men as they grapple with the realization that their upbringings were altered.
The hospital has denied the men's allegations. (Getty Images)

Unity Medical Center denied responsibility for the incident, asserting that an internal review yielded no evidence showing hospital personnel were at fault. However, the medical center did not dispute that the swap occurred.

The men said they knew that the DNA trail didn’t make sense, but that finding out they’ve been switched at birth was a huge revelation. (iStock)

title: FDA to review 7 popular peptides touted for weight loss, healing and longevity
summary: The FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee weighs peptides for obesity, insulin resistance, opioid withdrawal and insomnia this week.
story: Dr. Alex Tatem, a board-certified urologist in Indiana, discusses why upcoming federal hearings on seven peptides were mandated and argues that years of patient use show a promising safety profile.
The Food and Drug Administration is taking a closer look this week at seven unapproved peptide substances that have surged in popularity for their purported health benefits.

At meetings scheduled for July 23 and 24 at the FDA’s White Oak Campus in Silver Spring, Maryland, the FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee will consider whether to recommend adding seven peptide substances to the agency’s 503A Bulks List, which would allow them to be used in certain compounded prescription drugs.
Although these peptides are not FDA-approved, they are widely available through wellness clinics, compounding operations and gray-market online sellers.
THINKING ABOUT PEPTIDES? DOCTORS REVEAL KEY DOS AND DONT'S AS 'WILD WEST' MARKET GROWS

HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has voiced support for expanding access to certain peptide therapies, while FDA reviewers have raised concerns about the limited evidence supporting the safety and effectiveness of the seven substances under consideration.

According to Reuters, consumer demand is likely to "remain strong" despite the outcome, as peptides have surged in popularity for weight loss, muscle building, performance enhancement, chronic disease management and even wound repair.
Peptides have surged in popularity for weight loss, muscle building, performance enhancement, chronic disease management and even wound repair. (iStock)
FDA documents show that the following seven peptides are under review.
No. 1: BPC-157
Proposed use: Ulcerative colitis
Proposed forms: Oral capsules, nasal spray, injections, transdermal cream, rectal suppository
Proposed use: Wound healing
Proposed forms: Subcutaneous or intramuscular injection
SECRET TO WEIGHT LOSS MAY BE HIDING IN YOUR GUT, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS
No. 3: KPV
Proposed use: Wound healing and inflammatory condition
Proposed forms: Cream and gel
No. 4: MOTS-c
Proposed use: Obesity and osteoporosis
Proposed forms: Subcutaneous injection
No. 5: Semax
Proposed use: Cerebral ischemia (shortage of blood flow and oxygen to the brain), migraine and trigeminal neuralgia (chronic pain condition in the face)
Proposed form: Intranasal spray, subcutaneous injection
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
No. 6: Emideltide
Proposed use: Opioid withdrawal, chronic insomnia, narcolepsy
Proposed form: Subcutaneous injection
No. 7: Epitalon
Proposed use: Insomnia
Proposed form: Subcutaneous injection
"These were all medications that were designed to help people live well and live as healthy as possible," Tatem previously told Fox News Digital about peptides. (iStock)
Performance potential
Performance medicine and peptide expert Dr. Alex Tatem, a board-certified urologist and member of Rugiet's Medical Advisory Board, will testify at this week's FDA hearings.
In an interview with Fox News Digital, Indiana-based Tatem said that every product up for review is "exciting," as each targets a different problem faced by patients.

"BPC-157 or TB-500 are compounds that can help facilitate healing after injury and have been shown in multiple studies to be incredibly safe when administered — which is interesting when you compare that to the over-the-counter options that we use now for aches and pains, like ibuprofen," he said.

Although ibuprofen is available over the counter, the FDA warns that it can cause serious side effects — including stomach bleeding, kidney damage and cardiovascular complications — especially when used at high doses or for long periods.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Tatem claimed that millions of BPC-157 doses have been administered and that relatively few adverse events have been reported.

"There is no other drug on the market that had that sort of safety record," Tatem said. "And it's not because of any magic — it's because these are natural substances that our bodies make and are familiar with, so that's what gives them this incredible safety profile."
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. testifies during the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health hearing on June 24, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc)

The FDA, however, has publicly stated that there is not enough evidence from human clinical trials on the safety or efficacy of these drugs. FDA reviewers have also cautioned that a peptide’s similarity to a naturally occurring substance does not eliminate potential risks.
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel cautioned that these substances "need careful study."
"I am not convinced the data is fully there yet."
According to the doctor, RFK Jr. told Siegel in their latest interview that he believes "not all peptides are created equal, whereas some are helpful, others may not be and need further study."

"I agree with that," Siegel told Fox News Digital. "I’m concerned about the impact some may have on the kidneys. I would like to see rigorous clinical trials before approval. I am not convinced the data is fully there yet."
Next steps

Tatem said he expects the hearings to be a "hard-fought battle," but hopes committee members will consider what he described as real-world data from tens of millions of doses administered between 2014 and 2023. The data showed adverse event rates of "well under 0.1%," he added.
If the committee recommends inclusion, the FDA would still need to complete its review and rulemaking process before formally adding any of the substances to the 503A Bulks List.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
That list includes active ingredients that state-licensed pharmacies are legally permitted to use for compounding prescription drugs, Tatem said.

He also suggested that the FDA could place some substances under a more permissive enforcement category temporarily while the rulemaking process continues. (The agency has not announced that it intends to do so.)

"Ultimately, what we would hope is, before the end of the year, patients would be able to go to their doctor, work through maybe a telehealth provider, and then be able to get a prescription for this under monitored medical supervision," he said.
"The most important thing to take away is that your voice matters."

"The most important thing to take away is that your voice matters, because this committee is just issuing a recommendation to the FDA. The FDA can take it or leave it," Tatem noted. "Everything that happens afterward is still anyone's guess."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Tatem encourages people to reach out to their local representatives to request access to "safe, regulated peptides made here in the United States of America."
Fox News Digital reached out to the FDA and ibuprofen product manufacturer Haleon for comment.
